ann_84.text: Through this part, an international plan clearly raises the typical customer's predicted chance of leaving from about 3% to about 27%, and more daytime minutes clearly raise it steadily, from about 1% at 112 minutes to about 10% at 249 minutes.
Being in California or Washington rather than one of the states the part does not single out raises it to about 12% and 10% (on the training data only).

Montana and New Jersey slightly raise it to about 7%, Texas to about 6%, Maine to about 5% and nine other states to about 3% to 4%, while Vermont, Maryland, Alaska, New Hampshire and Pennsylvania slightly lower it to about 1% and Florida, Wisconsin, Missouri, Alabama and Mississippi to about 2% to 3% (on the training data only).
More evening minutes slightly raise it steadily, from about 1% at 138 minutes to about 5% at 266 minutes, and a voice-mail plan slightly lowers it to below 1%.

More voice-mail messages, international minutes, night-time minutes and daytime calls, a longer account and a higher night-time charge slightly raise it steadily, and an area code other than 415 slightly raises it (on the training data only).
More international calls slightly lower it steadily, each extra call taking off about the same, and more night-time calls slightly lower it in an uneven way (on the training data only).

ann_85.text: Through this part, customer-service calls (0 to 3) clearly raise the predicted chance of leaving in an uneven way, from about 1% to about 13% for the typical customer it acts on (one with 2 customer-service calls and about 129 daytime minutes).

A higher daytime charge (19.07 to 42.40 US dollars) clearly lowers it in stages, and even more so for customers with more than one customer-service call: from about 18% to about 3%, against about 9% to about 3%.
It also clearly lowers it in stages, and more so, in New Hampshire: from about 24% to about 1% there, against about 9% to about 3% in most states.

The daytime charge lowers it only while it stays below about 25.31 US dollars, and in an uneven way across customers: for the typical customer, going from 15.49 to 59.76 US dollars moves it from about 14% to about 3% (on the training data only).
This part acts on 1292 of 4000 customers, 185 of whom left, and for the typical one it slightly raises the chance from about 1% to about 5%.
For that customer, being in New Hampshire raises it from about 5% to about 28% (on the training data only).

ann_86.text: Through this part, customer-service calls clearly add to the predicted chance of leaving from 3 calls upwards, in an uneven way: for a typical such customer, going from 0 to 4 calls moves it from about 3% to about 12%.
For the typical customer, calls (0 to 3) slightly raise it, in an uneven way, to about 4%.

For a typical customer with 3 customer-service calls (one in Idaho), a higher daytime charge slightly lowers it, mostly in a jump around 32.03 US dollars, where this part switches on: from about 4% to about 3% (on the training data only).

ann_87.text: Through this part, more daytime minutes raise the predicted chance of leaving: nothing until about 216 minutes, where this part switches on, then steadily; for the typical customer, going from 0 to 271 minutes moves it from about 3% to about 10% (on the training data only).

This part acts on 1002 of 4000 customers, 285 of whom left; for the typical one (a customer in Alabama with about 242 daytime minutes) it raises the chance from about 7% to about 12% (on the training data only).

Over the usual range, daytime minutes slightly raise it, nothing until about 216 minutes, then steadily: from about 3% at 112 minutes to about 6% at 249 minutes for the typical customer (on the training data only).
It slightly dampens the daytime-minutes effect in New York, where the rise still comes slowly at first, then faster: from about 1% to about 18% there, against about 1% to about 21% elsewhere.

ann_88.text: Through this part, a longer account raises the predicted chance of leaving only slightly: nothing until about 147, where this part switches on, then steadily; the typical customer stays at about 3% (on the training data only).

This part acts on 488 of 4000 customers, 77 of whom left; for the typical one (a customer in Oregon with an account length of 163) it slightly raises the chance from about 3% to about 4% (on the training data only).

ann_89.text: Through this part, being in Maryland raises the typical customer's predicted chance of leaving from about 3% to about 12% (on the training data only).
This part acts on 3918 of 4000 customers, 547 of whom left; for the typical one it lowers the chance from about 12% to about 3% (on the training data only).
Through the main part of the model, Maryland instead slightly lowers it to about 1% (on the training data only).

ann_90.text: Through this part, being in Louisiana or Missouri slightly raises the predicted chance of leaving to about 3%, and Ohio slightly lowers it, staying at about 3% (on the training data only).

ann_91.text: One small part barely changes the predictions.

ann_92.text: Across the whole model, an international plan clearly raises the typical customer's predicted chance of leaving from about 3% to about 27%.

More daytime minutes raise it slowly at first, then faster: for the typical customer it clearly goes from about 1% at 112 minutes to about 21% at 249 minutes, flattening out near the bottom because it cannot go much lower.
A higher daytime charge clearly lowers it in an uneven way, from about 9% at 19.07 US dollars to about 3% at 42.40 US dollars.
Being in California or Washington rather than one of the states the model does not single out raises it to about 12% and 10% (on the training data only).

Montana and New Jersey slightly raise it to about 7%, Texas to about 6%, Maine to about 5% and eleven other states to about 3% to 4%, while Vermont, Alaska and Pennsylvania slightly lower it to about 1% and Florida, Wisconsin, Alabama, Missouri, Mississippi and New York to about 2% to 3% (on the training data only).

More evening minutes slightly raise it steadily, from about 1% at 138 minutes to about 5% at 266 minutes, customer-service calls (0 to 3) slightly raise it in an uneven way to about 4%, a voice-mail plan slightly lowers it to below 1%, and the model ignores evening calls, the evening charge and the international charge.

More voice-mail messages, international minutes, night-time minutes and daytime calls and a higher night-time charge slightly raise it steadily, a longer account slightly raises it slowly at first, then faster, and an area code other than 415 slightly raises it (on the training data only).
More international calls slightly lower it steadily, each extra call taking off about the same, and more night-time calls slightly lower it in an uneven way (on the training data only).

ann_84.original: Hypothesis: additive logit backbone (identity node over the 38 direct input->output edges). Formula: 0.107 accountLength + 0.744 internationalPlan - 0.841 voiceMailPlan + 0.297 numberVmailMessages + 1.105 totalDayMinutes + 0.115 totalDayCalls + 0.500 totalEveMinutes + 0.174 totalNightMinutes + 0.050 totalNightCharge (identical to night minutes after z-scoring, net +0.22) - 0.010 totalNightCalls + 0.317 totalIntlMinutes - 0.211 totalIntlCalls - 0.002 areaCode415 + 25 state offsets (|w|<=0.22 per z, e.g. state:46 -0.22, state:47 +0.18, state:4 +0.16). Evidence: exact closed form; sensitivity summary equals |weights|; one-hot offsets: internationalPlan +2.54 logit, voiceMailPlan -1.91 (both match their calibrating offsets on train). numberCustomerServiceCalls has no direct edge: its whole effect runs through the two gates. totalDayCharge is not used directly; totalDayMinutes is (they are identical after z-scoring).
ann_84.proposed: A main part that sums separate effects, in which an international plan (about 3% to 27%) and daytime minutes (steadily, about 1% to 10%) raise the chance of leaving and a voice-mail plan slightly lowers it; state and other usage effects are slight or seen on the training data only.

ann_85.original: Hypothesis (supported): customer-service-calls x low-day-usage interaction. 104 = relu(0.576 + 0.755 CSC + 1.309 relu(0.332 CSC - 0.212) - 0.862 dayCharge - 1.939 relu(1.429 dayCharge + 1.216) + 0.206 state30 + 0.006 state6 + 1.688 h2039), read out 0.617*h104 + 0.688*relu(0.980 h104 - 0.618). Logit grows ~0.7-1.4 per service call and falls with day charge (slope -3.6 per z while 4834 is on), reaching zero above the day-charge median. Evidence (train, 4000 rows): mean contribution 1.13 (0 calls) to 6.97 (6 calls) in the lowest day-charge decile, 0 above p50 for <=4 calls; active on 32% of rows; sensitivity dominated by dayCharge (0.64) and CSC (0.29). For low-call, low-usage customers it cancels the negative part of the linear dayMinutes slope (+1.105 per z), so day usage below p75 has an almost flat net effect. Side inputs: state30 shifts 104 (row effect -0.85..+1.13, mean -0.15 net of its direct edge); 2039 (state9-gated) is active on only 3 train rows (CSC 8-9). Linearising this child alone costs 0.012 train AUC; restoring it alone to the all-linear model gains 0.050.
ann_85.proposed: Customer-service calls with low daytime charge: calls raise the chance of leaving in an uneven way (about 1% to 13% for the customers it acts on), and a higher daytime charge lowers it in stages, more so with more than one call and in New Hampshire.

ann_86.original: Hypothesis (supported): a second service-calls threshold gated off by high day charge. 7506 = relu(-0.687 + 0.739 CSC - 2.266 relu(0.859 dayCharge - 0.133)), read out 1.195*h7506 + 1.451*relu(0.242 + 0.773 h7506) (9029 always on: constant 0.35 plus net slope 2.32 on h7506). Evidence (train): +0.35 constant for 0-2 calls; from 3 calls it adds ~+1.3 logit per extra call when day charge is below its median, much less in p50-75 and nothing above p75 (except 7+ calls). Active on 12.8% of rows. Together with csc_low_day_gate the model matches the empirical pattern: CSC>=4 & day charge <p25 churn 0.90-1.00 (model 0.81-0.84); CSC>=4 & day charge >p50 churn 0.19-0.20 (model 0.20-0.25); CSC 0-3 churn 0.04-0.06 below p75 (model 0.05-0.07). The two gates are largely redundant: linearising either alone costs only 0.012-0.013 AUC, both together 0.063.
ann_86.proposed: A customer-service part that adds to the chance of leaving from 3 calls upwards, in an uneven way (about 3% to 12% at 4 calls), slightly weakened by a higher daytime charge, mostly in a jump around 32.03 US dollars.

ann_87.original: Hypothesis (supported): high-usage hinge. 6238 = relu(-0.508 + 0.769 dayMinutes - 0.018 state34), read out 1.725. Zero for the bottom ~75% of day minutes (z<0.66), +0.36 logit at p75-90 and +1.46 above p90, where churn is 0.49 vs 0.06-0.15 below. Adds to the linear +1.105 day-minutes slope (dayMinutes == dayCharge after z-scoring, so this and the dayCharge gates read the same quantity). state34's weight is negligible (row effect <=0.21). Restoring it alone to the all-linear model gains 0.023 train AUC; linearising it alone costs 0.002.
ann_87.proposed: A heavy daytime-usage part: nothing until about 216 minutes, then steadily (about 3% to 10%), on the training data only.

ann_88.original: Hypothesis (weakly supported, nearly inert): 11575 = relu(1.055 accountLength - 1.232), read out 0.262: an extra slope for the 12% longest-tenure accounts (z>1.17), on top of the direct +0.107 slope. Evidence: contribution <=0.25 logit; linearising it changes train AUC by 0.0001; churn rate is not clearly higher at long tenure, so this looks like a small fitted bend rather than a real effect.
ann_88.proposed: A small extra account-length part: nothing until about 147, then steadily; all effects slight and seen on the training data only.

ann_89.original: Hypothesis (supported): exact state-20 offset implemented as a near-cancelling pair. 4253 = relu(0.841 - 0.818 state20) is 0.959 for every non-state-20 row and 0 for state 20's 82 rows; read out -1.645, so state 20 adds +1.58 via this unit and -1.18 via its direct edge: net +0.40 on 82 rows (19 churners, 23%). Raw empirical log-odds offset +0.62; calibrating offset given other features +0.35, so the net offset is calibrated on train. Linear fit is exact (binary input).
ann_89.proposed: A Maryland switch that raises the chance of leaving to about 12%, largely offset by the backbone's lowering for Maryland, on the training data only.

ann_90.original: Hypothesis (supported): exact single-state offsets. 11955 = relu(1.002 state18 - 0.698) fires only for state 18 (65 rows): +0.17 logit (net state18 +0.18); 11236 = relu(0.997 state24 + 1.999) and 1084 = relu(0.0068 state35 + 0.059) are always positive, i.e. affine (state24 unit +0.07, net state24 -0.28; state35 unit -0.007, net +0.48). Linear fits are exact; contribution to AUC nil.
ann_90.proposed: Slight adjustments for Louisiana, Missouri and Ohio, on the training data only.

ann_91.original: Hypothesis (supported): dead units. 6958 = relu(-0.311 - 0.238 state15) and 2730 = relu(-0.895 - 0.541 state5 + 0.169 h6958) have negative pre-activations for both values of their one-hot inputs, so they are zero on every possible row and contribute exactly 0 (states 5 and 15 have no effect in this network).
ann_91.proposed: Switched-off units that barely change the predictions.

ann_92.original: Hypothesis (supported): P(churn) = sigmoid(-2.455 + linear_backbone + csc_low_day_gate + csc_threshold_low_day + day_minutes_hinge + account_length_hinge + state20_switch + minor_state_units + dead_state_chain); all children combine additively in the output logit; the 27 unconnected inputs (incl. totalEveCharge, totalIntlCharge, areaCode 408/510, 23 states) have zero effect. The non-linear structure is a single idea: customer-service calls only raise churn risk when day usage is low-to-medium, and day usage only raises risk at the top quartile. summary.text: For a typical customer (one in West Virginia with area code 415, an account length of 100, no international or voice-mail plan, one customer-service call and median usage such as 180 daytime minutes), the model predicts about a 3% chance that the customer leaves, and an international plan clearly raises that to about 27%.

More daytime minutes clearly raise it slowly at first, then faster, from about 1% at 112 minutes to about 21% at 249 minutes, while a higher daytime charge clearly lowers it in an uneven way, from about 9% at 19.07 US dollars to about 3% at 42.40 US dollars.
Through one part, customer-service calls clearly add to it from 3 calls upwards, in an uneven way: for a typical such customer, going from 0 to 4 calls moves it from about 3% to about 12%.

In another part, customer-service calls clearly raise it in an uneven way, from about 1% to about 13% for the typical customer that part acts on (one with 2 customer-service calls and about 129 daytime minutes), and a higher daytime charge clearly lowers it in stages, more for customers with more than one call: from about 18% to about 3%, against about 9% to about 3%.
Being in California or Washington rather than one of the states the model does not single out raises it to about 10% to 12% (on the training data only).

A voice-mail plan slightly lowers it to below 1%, more evening minutes slightly raise it steadily, from about 1% at 138 minutes to about 5% at 266 minutes, and the model ignores evening calls, the evening charge and the international charge.

parts.name: full_model
parts.original_hypothesis: Hypothesis (supported): P(churn) = sigmoid(-2.455 + linear_backbone + csc_low_day_gate + csc_threshold_low_day + day_minutes_hinge + account_length_hinge + state20_switch + minor_state_units + dead_state_chain); all children combine additively in the output logit; the 27 unconnected inputs (incl. totalEveCharge, totalIntlCharge, areaCode 408/510, 23 states) have zero effect. The non-linear structure is a single idea: customer-service calls only raise churn risk when day usage is low-to-medium, and day usage only raises risk at the top quartile. Evidence (train): AUC 0.9006; all children linearised 0.8352 (refit LR 0.8433); the two CSC x low-day gates restore 0.0634 of the 0.0654 gap together, +day hinge 0.0652; state units are exact one-hot offsets (all states off: AUC 0.8933). SHAP (300 rows, probability scale): linear backbone 0.129, 104 0.039, 6238 0.032, 7664 0.030, 7506 0.015, 9029 0.014, 4253 0.003, others <0.003.
variables: number of calls to customer service

parts.name: linear_backbone
parts.original_hypothesis: Hypothesis: additive logit backbone (identity node over the 38 direct input->output edges). Formula: 0.107 accountLength + 0.744 internationalPlan - 0.841 voiceMailPlan + 0.297 numberVmailMessages + 1.105 totalDayMinutes + 0.115 totalDayCalls + 0.500 totalEveMinutes + 0.174 totalNightMinutes + 0.050 totalNightCharge (identical to night minutes after z-scoring, net +0.22) - 0.010 totalNightCalls + 0.317 totalIntlMinutes - 0.211 totalIntlCalls - 0.002 areaCode415 + 25 state offsets (|w|<=0.22 per z, e.g. state:46 -0.22, state:47 +0.18, state:4 +0.16). Evidence: exact closed form; sensitivity summary equals |weights|; one-hot offsets: internationalPlan +2.54 logit, voiceMailPlan -1.91 (both match their calibrating offsets on train). numberCustomerServiceCalls has no direct edge: its whole effect runs through the two gates. totalDayCharge is not used directly; totalDayMinutes is (they are identical after z-scoring).

parts.name: csc_low_day_gate
parts.original_hypothesis: Hypothesis (supported): customer-service-calls x low-day-usage interaction. 104 = relu(0.576 + 0.755 CSC + 1.309 relu(0.332 CSC - 0.212) - 0.862 dayCharge - 1.939 relu(1.429 dayCharge + 1.216) + 0.206 state30 + 0.006 state6 + 1.688 h2039), read out 0.617*h104 + 0.688*relu(0.980 h104 - 0.618). Logit grows ~0.7-1.4 per service call and falls with day charge (slope -3.6 per z while 4834 is on), reaching zero above the day-charge median. Evidence (train, 4000 rows): mean contribution 1.13 (0 calls) to 6.97 (6 calls) in the lowest day-charge decile, 0 above p50 for <=4 calls; active on 32% of rows; sensitivity dominated by dayCharge (0.64) and CSC (0.29). For low-call, low-usage customers it cancels the negative part of the linear dayMinutes slope (+1.105 per z), so day usage below p75 has an almost flat net effect. Side inputs: state30 shifts 104 (row effect -0.85..+1.13, mean -0.15 net of its direct edge); 2039 (state9-gated) is active on only 3 train rows (CSC 8-9). Linearising this child alone costs 0.012 train AUC; restoring it alone to the all-linear model gains 0.050.
variables: number of calls to customer service

parts.name: csc_threshold_low_day
parts.original_hypothesis: Hypothesis (supported): a second service-calls threshold gated off by high day charge. 7506 = relu(-0.687 + 0.739 CSC - 2.266 relu(0.859 dayCharge - 0.133)), read out 1.195*h7506 + 1.451*relu(0.242 + 0.773 h7506) (9029 always on: constant 0.35 plus net slope 2.32 on h7506). Evidence (train): +0.35 constant for 0-2 calls; from 3 calls it adds ~+1.3 logit per extra call when day charge is below its median, much less in p50-75 and nothing above p75 (except 7+ calls). Active on 12.8% of rows. Together with csc_low_day_gate the model matches the empirical pattern: CSC>=4 & day charge <p25 churn 0.90-1.00 (model 0.81-0.84); CSC>=4 & day charge >p50 churn 0.19-0.20 (model 0.20-0.25); CSC 0-3 churn 0.04-0.06 below p75 (model 0.05-0.07). The two gates are largely redundant: linearising either alone costs only 0.012-0.013 AUC, both together 0.063.
variables: number of calls to customer service

parts.name: day_minutes_hinge
parts.original_hypothesis: Hypothesis (supported): high-usage hinge. 6238 = relu(-0.508 + 0.769 dayMinutes - 0.018 state34), read out 1.725. Zero for the bottom ~75% of day minutes (z<0.66), +0.36 logit at p75-90 and +1.46 above p90, where churn is 0.49 vs 0.06-0.15 below. Adds to the linear +1.105 day-minutes slope (dayMinutes == dayCharge after z-scoring, so this and the dayCharge gates read the same quantity). state34's weight is negligible (row effect <=0.21). Restoring it alone to the all-linear model gains 0.023 train AUC; linearising it alone costs 0.002.

parts.name: state20_switch
parts.original_hypothesis: Hypothesis (supported): exact state-20 offset implemented as a near-cancelling pair. 4253 = relu(0.841 - 0.818 state20) is 0.959 for every non-state-20 row and 0 for state 20's 82 rows; read out -1.645, so state 20 adds +1.58 via this unit and -1.18 via its direct edge: net +0.40 on 82 rows (19 churners, 23%). Raw empirical log-odds offset +0.62; calibrating offset given other features +0.35, so the net offset is calibrated on train. Linear fit is exact (binary input).

parts.name: account_length_hinge
parts.original_hypothesis: Hypothesis (weakly supported, nearly inert): 11575 = relu(1.055 accountLength - 1.232), read out 0.262: an extra slope for the 12% longest-tenure accounts (z>1.17), on top of the direct +0.107 slope. Evidence: contribution <=0.25 logit; linearising it changes train AUC by 0.0001; churn rate is not clearly higher at long tenure, so this looks like a small fitted bend rather than a real effect.

parts.name: minor_state_units
parts.original_hypothesis: Hypothesis (supported): exact single-state offsets. 11955 = relu(1.002 state18 - 0.698) fires only for state 18 (65 rows): +0.17 logit (net state18 +0.18); 11236 = relu(0.997 state24 + 1.999) and 1084 = relu(0.0068 state35 + 0.059) are always positive, i.e. affine (state24 unit +0.07, net state24 -0.28; state35 unit -0.007, net +0.48). Linear fits are exact; contribution to AUC nil.

parts.name: dead_state_chain
parts.original_hypothesis: Hypothesis (supported): dead units. 6958 = relu(-0.311 - 0.238 state15) and 2730 = relu(-0.895 - 0.541 state5 + 0.169 h6958) have negative pre-activations for both values of their one-hot inputs, so they are zero on every possible row and contribute exactly 0 (states 5 and 15 have no effect in this network).
